title: Introduction to C#
learningObjectives: Define C# as a general-purpose, strongly typed programming language.
Describe common uses of C# across application types.
Explain the relationship between C# source and the .NET platform.
Distinguish language features from frameworks and workloads.
Identify trade-offs involving portability, dependencies and runtime requirements.

understand.concept: C# (pronounced C sharp) is a modern, general-purpose programming language developed by Microsoft. It is commonly used with .NET to build console tools, web services, desktop software, cloud applications, games and cross-platform applications. The language provides types, methods, classes, interfaces, pattern matching and asynchronous constructs.
understand.whyItMatters: C# supports application development across several domains while teaching transferable engineering concepts such as type safety, encapsulation, testing and dependency management.
understand.analogy: C# is like a precise vocabulary and grammar for describing a program; .NET supplies reusable tools and services that help the program operate.
understand.analogyLimit: A language does not automatically provide every application feature. A web API, game or desktop application still needs suitable frameworks, packages, configuration and a target runtime.

explain.narrative:
## What C# is

C# is a compiled, statically and strongly typed language in the .NET ecosystem. Types help the compiler detect many invalid operations before a program runs. C# supports object-oriented, functional and component-oriented programming styles.

## Where it is used

C# is used for command-line applications, web applications and APIs with ASP.NET Core, desktop applications, cloud services, games and tooling. The appropriate workload depends on platform requirements and project constraints.

## C# and .NET

C# is the language. .NET is a development platform that includes a runtime, libraries and SDK tooling. ASP.NET Core, .NET MAUI and game engines are separate frameworks or platforms that can use C#.

## Portability and trade-offs

Modern .NET supports multiple operating systems, but portability still depends on APIs, native dependencies, deployment settings and target platforms.
